utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. For the record, accused Popovic is not present this morning. The Chamber was duly notified about this in the course of last week, and a waiver has been filed with the Registry. The other accused are present. Prosecution today, it's Mr. McCloskey. Absentees from the Defence teams, I notice Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Gosnell, I saw Mr. Davis -- yes, he is here. Okay. So that's it. I take it there are no preliminaries, so we can start with your cross-examination, Mr. McCloskey. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had a good weekend. We are proceeding and concluding with your cross-examination this morning and then you are free to go back home. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And my name is Peter McCloskey. I represent the Prosecution. First thing, after having a chance to think about what you had said over the weekend, is there anything you want to change from your direct testimony, any mistakes you made or anything you want to change?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only mistake could have been the sentence that General Gvero uttered in conversation with General Mladic to the effect that the two Serb towns had fallen but they were falling, they fell on the 28th, and this sentence was uttered before that; but they had been in a process of being lost for the six preceding months. So this is the only thing I want to rectify so I'm not misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you do recall saying twice to Mr. Krgovic that those two towns had -- had fallen, past tense, and then Mr. Krgovic tried to remind you and say "falling," and so you've had a chance to think about that and now you want to go with what Mr. Krgovic said. That's the correct way, "falling," and not "fell."

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Because you know that if General Gvero had said to General Mladic on the 26th of July that that they had fallen, he couldn't have said it on the 26th, he would have had to said that from Zepa or Han Pijesak area after they had fallen, so it would have been on or after the 28th. So you've now corrected that on the record, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's -- can you tell me, did you have a chance to look at your flight log, your flight records? I think we all know here that pilots and flight engineers are always judged and based on their flight times, and those logs and those records are essential to be kept, and that surely you're an active flight officer today as we've learned. So surely you've had a chance to go over your flight logs before testifying about those important flights of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go over them for one reason: The flight log and the flight record of each member of the crew is maintained in a very precise manner in peacetime. I and many of my colleagues were shabby in maintaining our flight records, simply because it was impossible to enter data after flights every day because flight records were maintained in Banja Luka, and I was dislocated in another part of the country. We recorded those on -- in notebooks on scraps of paper and then subsequently they would be entered into logbooks. Almost 30 per cent of my flights have not been recorded because I lost the notes, and I could not reconstruct them from memory. Before coming here to testify, I have not seen any records. I recall that that period was special because we flew every day. There were no breaks in our flight duty. We had 10 to 15 days of flying every day without respite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you're aware that the Serbian government is cooperating with this Tribunal and provides military documents frequently to us and that we will ask for your flight records. So you may want to think about that. We have seen records in this case of the simplest TAM-110 truck keeping track of the fuel, let alone flight fuel. Certainly, sir, you've had a chance to look at some flight record before coming here. It's a serious question, and what you're doing is very serious.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready, in respect of all the documentation that I hold or my state holds, to hand them over to you, and I'm sure I can prove that on that date I was at Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, how many helicopters, operational helicopters, did the VRS have in July 1995 -- did the Main Staff have, not just the VRS but the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka there was only one helicopter, and most of the time during the war there was only one helicopter. Are you interested in the make or some technical data about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I think you told us it was a Gazelle, that's the make; right? And what year was it manufactured?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The helicopter that I flew during that period, he had the military markings 12882, which means the 800 series, and the helicopter that I flew was manufactured immediately before the war. I saw the documents, but I forgot it. So the 800 to 900 series were produced towards the end of the 1980s at the Sokar [phoen] factory in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many other pilots, how many pilots were there that actually could fly that helicopter? I'm not talking about flight engineers now, I'm talking about pilots.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Crna Rijeka you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Crna Rijeka, at that time, there were two pilots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Dusan Maran, who flew together with me through most of the war, and his substitute was major and later Lieutenant-General Trivo Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was with you on the 26th July flight that we've seen?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Dusan Maran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And besides yourself, how many other flight engineers were there?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Crna Rijeka, at the Main Staff, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you trained to be able to fly that helicopter if you'd had to?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no training in airforce for me to be -- to enable me to fly on my own, but Major Maran had an assistant to train me for -- to able to fly on my own if in case he was hurt, so I was trained unofficially to pilot the aircraft on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the aircraft can be piloted from the left side of the -- the aircraft if need be; correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it has double commands identical on the left-hand side and the right-hand side. On the right-hand side seats, that's the pilot seat, and on the left-hand side is the flight engineer seat, but the commands are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many passengers can be taken if the first two seats are filled by you and the pilot, how many can fit in the backseat?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three passengers can sit at the back, a maximum of three passengers, and there is some room for luggage; but as for passengers, there could have been three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you must have been aware of UN Resolution 781 that was enacted in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I roughly know what it's all about. I don't know everything that was written in it, but I remember the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, what was the gist of it as would have been known by people that were -- were flying in RS air-space during the war?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that resolution concerned prohibition of flights over the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, concerning the Republika Srpska Air Force. I'm not sure whether any other air forces were banned, but we were, and that no-flight zone was respected in terms of combat aircraft. Fighters and bombers did not fly. Helicopters did, mainly transporting the wounded, military commanders, and politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that no-flight resolution affect the way you -- that plane -- excuse me, that helicopter was flown?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It affected in terms that we had to be mindful not to be shot down by fighter planes. We did not know who was in charge of the airspace of BH, but we had to be mindful not to be shot down, and this meant the flight elevation, the route. Sometimes we would land when we spotted a fighter plane and wait for it to disappear. Sometimes it resulted in the wounded dying because we had to wait for the fighter planes, and we were transporting such wounding to a hospital for surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see you flying at the tree top levels when you were flying General Mladic, that is because you were concerned about the no-flight restrictions and being shot down by NATO?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you saw was unsecurely high. We used to fly even lower. But on that flight, we were not afraid of being shot down by NATO, but by our own anti-aircraft defence, which was stationed around the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you lived in the barracks there at Crna Rijeka; correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you knew that a Muslim sabotage group had actually gotten pretty close to the barracks in June 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, relatively close.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you knew that those hills around Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka, Zepa, densely wooded mountains, had potential saboteurs, Muslim saboteurs, in them armed with Zolja shoulder fire rockets, automatic weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the area of Zepa, but we never flew over the area of Zepa. We flew around Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka, Borik, up to Boksanica. We did not fly over Zepa. There was this possibility of saboteurs opening fire from the woods or different positions, but we had an advantage in that we had mufflers on exhaust pipes of the engine, so you could not hear the helicopter approaching, only when it was flying away. So they had to be very trained to recognise and hear the helicopter. We changed routes every day for security reasons. We knew safe routes to approach Boksanica, and we used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My point is that it was a very dangerous job. When that helicopter went up, you were facing a grave threat with a very valuable machine and cargo, potentially?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now in July, where you've said already that you remembered the flights, and you especially remember the 26th of July, in July 1995, were you and the pilot you've mentioned, sorry, I've forgot his name, what was his name again, the last name?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Dusan Maran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you and Major Maran the only people that flew General Mladic around in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were the only ones who transported him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who, besides General Mladic, did you transport in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, July is a long month. Can you narrow it down? Do you mean the incidents of the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I just mean -- you've said you remembered the flights, so I'm sure you've thought about July. What other Main Staff Generals, if any, did you fly around in July; Tolimir, Gvero, Miletic, Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July, in that period, we flew General Tolimir, General Krstic, some people from the press centre, cameramen, interpreters. There were only -- even journalists writing for Serb newspapers would come and wanted to report and cover the story, and this is where we came in to fly them. Generals Gvero and Milovanovic I did not transport. They did not appear up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you must remember when General Mladic and others walked into Srebrenica on the 11th of July, 1995. It was all over the Serb television; correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that period. We did not take part in that action with our helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we have a -- a report of the Bratunac Brigade at 65 ter 237 - I don't want to spend the time to go to it - but it indicates that General Mladic was in the area of the Bratunac Brigade on -- on 10 July. Did you fly him there to that little airfield just outside Bratunac on 10 July?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not transport him on the 10th of July because the weather conditions around Crna Rijeka and Han Pijesak, that part of Romanija, were not conducive to flying helicopter. Had the weather conditions been different, we would have, but we did not takeoff because it was not safe even for a short flight, let alone a long flight to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about on the 11th of July? General Mladic again is in the Bratunac area on the 11th of July. We know it was safe for aircraft to fly on the 11th because NATO bombed Srebrenica then. Did you take him on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I could not now explain meteorology, which tells to an ordinary man that in one town you can have ideal conditions, while at the same time, in a nearby town, you can have the conditions that prevent any flying. The Gazelle helicopter, which was produced in Britain and France, and, therefore, you can check all of its parameters, all of its conditions, it simply is not equipped to fly under very complex weather conditions. So in a helicopter, for example, we did not have any de-icing system, and if you fly into a cloud, you need that. We also did not have any equipment for night flights. So it was very limited in what it could do, and also our crews were not trained to fly under very complex weather conditions. But in the period that you just described, we did have, for several days, a complex weather conditions. The so-called QGOs, and this was true of the region of Crna Rijeka and the region in which we were. A flight aircraft which takes off from Italy was fully equipped, and it flew at higher elevations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it was a simple question: Did you take him to the Bratunac area on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We also know that General Mladic was in Belgrade on the 14th and 15th meeting with President Milosevic, and I'm sure he didn't drive all the way to Belgrade. Did you fly him to Belgrade for that -- that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can answer without being interrupted, Mr. Prosecutor, I remember that flight to Belgrade. The general ordered that we had to go to Belgrade urgently for some significant talks. He didn't tell us who he was going to meet. The pilot, Major Maran, informed him that the weather conditions were not such as to guarantee a safe flight from Crna Rijeka, but he ordered that we had to take off. So we prepared a helicopter and we took off. The helicopter, which usually covers 3 kilometres in a minute, we flew 45 to 50 minutes to cover 3 kilometres. So we simply -- simply hovered because the fog was so dense. We tried to go towards Vlasenica. We saw the weather conditions would be better there on the mountain slope of Romanija; however, we had to land in a valley, literally in a brook. The general was very upset. He yelled at us saying he was going to be late for the meeting. Only then he noticed that we only had our personal weapons. I had a revolver, the major had a pistol, and he tried to cross the woods with Major Maran, to the roads, the main roads between Vlasenica and Han Pijesak, there they stopped a vehicle which returned them to Han Pijesak, and from there, he took off in a car and went to Belgrade. I stayed by the helicopter for nearly an entire day waiting for the weather conditions to improve as to allow me to takeoff and go to the base in which we were stationed, which were some 3 kilometres away. In the meantime, the military police security came to secure my position, because at that time, the Muslim forces were also breaking through those particular areas. And, obviously, Major Maran came back, and he flew off with me. I believe this was on the 13th or the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you'll always have the ability to explain any answer, and lawyers - and especially prosecutors - may sometimes interrupt if they think we're not getting at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What day did you takeoff to try to get Mladic to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 13th or the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning hours, could be around 9.00 or 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the 26th of July. We saw the -- a bit of the flight, and you've identified yourself in that helicopter as the flight engineer as you were going towards the Boksanica site. Did you watch the whole video, they showed you the whole video?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what "entire video" comprises, but I saw a bit more than this very moment. I know that a part of the flight that preceded that was also filmed, and later on when we arrived at Boksanica, but I'm not sure what the whole video comprises. But let me just say that I was shown more than what we could see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you've said you can't be seen anywhere on the video at Boksanica, and you went into a long explanation that you made a special effort to stay out of the front of the camera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if you've seen the video, surely you recall seeing that after Mladic was dropped off at Boksanica, he turned around and waves goodbye and the helicopter flies off. Are you telling us you stayed behind while that helicopter flew off into this very dangerous space with no engineering officer? Or did you, maybe, just go get some fuel or put the helicopter in a safer spot or something like that?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that the area of Boksanica was as dangerous to prevent Major Maran from leaving the region on his own. I stayed behind, I assume, for the following reason: Because he had to go and get some other passengers, and if there were four passengers, this way he could fit them all in without flying twice. It only required five or ten minutes of flight. When you are asking about the fuel, we would always fill-in the reservoir in the evening, at the end of the day, in order for the helicopter to be able to fly to Banja Luka in the morning with the full reservoir. So the only reason why I stayed behind was that he could go and get more passengers and nothing bad could happen to him on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you say "I assume," so you don't know.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure, as I can't be sure of many other things, but I'm just saying why it would happen for a pilot to fly on his own because this happened on several occasions, and this would have been one of the reasons. If you had to take four passengers, then it was easier to fly only once instead of flying twice bringing in three persons on one occasion and then additional person on the second occasion. As you said yourself, this was a dangerous area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who did he go to bring back? It must have been pretty important if they are going to leave a perfectly good flight engineer just hanging around and fly this very expensive machine. Who did he bring back?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it must have been somebody from the Main Staff, or possibly interpreters. As I said previously, the general came in with a cameramen, so I assume the interpreters had to be brought in from the press centre, possibly somebody else, General Tolimir or somebody else, but it must have been somebody important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Possibly he went to pick up the general's escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it possible you went with him? And if you don't really know, it's certainly possible you went with him and came back later.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I stayed behind in the region of Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You clearly remember that, but you don't have a clear memory of who he brought back. How is that?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day we transported passengers several times between Boksanica and Crna Rijeka or Boksanica and Han Pijesak. I can't remember all the passengers, but I do remember that I was left behind because I was left behind on all of these days. It wasn't the first time it happened. I would normally be left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's normal to fly every day to Boksanica and leave the flight engineer and go back into that air-space where there is Muslims, there is your own troops, and there is NATO, no flight engineer, and coming back with very valuable cargo such as General Tolimir with no flight engineer? Come on, sir.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, a Gazelle helicopter is a light-transport helicopter. It had no defence weapons, so if anybody was to shoot at us, be it a fighter plane or an infantry man from the woods, we could simply look at them and give them sort of a mean look. There was nothing we could do about this, and for that reason they did not need a flight engineer. A pilot was enough to fly the aircraft, and exactly as you said, this was a dangerous zone, and this is why we tried to decrease the number of flights and increase the number of passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned, briefly, on Friday remembering a -- a meeting with General Smith and General Mladic at the Jela Restaurant, and we know from this trial that there was a meeting - as we can see from a UN report at 65 ter 2943 - of a meeting between General Mladic, Tolimir, and Smith. And I want to show you a few blurbs on that because, again, it was caught on video, and I think you will see yourself again on video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could, again, go to 65 ter 4590, and as we are doing that, I'll just read back due what you said:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Well, it was my personal position in terms of being in photographs and being recorded in any way -- well, I'm simply not in favour of that. I don't have an inclination. I don't want to be photographed or filmed, so throughout the war, I always tried to be behind the camera. I didn't want to have my face, my photograph taken, that's simply not something that I craved. So from the time we got off the helicopter, I was always behind the cameramen, but I was also close to General Mladic who was moving about the clearing." Emphasis, my own, obviously not yours. And we'll just start with a few blurbs to see if you can recollect any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We started off with a brief little meeting where you could see General Mladic and General Smith, do you know if you were ever inside that building seeing any part of that? I know it wasn't much, so ...

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not witness any part of the meeting, so those of us who belonged to the escort were not allowed in, neither those of us who were members of the crew of Mr. Mladic or Mr. Mladic's security, nor the security of General Smith. We all stayed in the parking-lot, and when we were informed that the meeting was over, then we went to the region of Boksanica. So we approached the helicopter. This helicopter was across the street from the Jela Motel, maybe some 50 metres from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as we look at this still that's there at 00.00.13, does that look roughly across the field from the Jela that you remember?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we can now see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is across the road from the Jela Motel, so there was a small parking-lot, the road, and then this field where we landed with our helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know your back was to the -- to the cameraman, but was that you, your left side that, you know, we saw immediately preceding -- we'll just go back. I'm sorry. Right there, which is 00.00.34.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is me. My seat was on the left-hand side. I was standing by the helicopter, and we were preparing the helicopter for the take off. I guess that I brought in the general's staff and I was preparing the seat for the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so where is your next destination? Do you know as you're preparing the seat, do you know where you're going next? Have you been told yet?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pilot knew that. He was told that in front of the motel. He was told where we were to go. Then the general turned and invited General Smith to go with him on the helicopter. He said it was easier to fly on a helicopter than to go by car, but General Smith refused that. I'm not sure if he joined us later on, but he went -- he was invited to Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did -- you said part of your duties was navigation. Did you help get the craft to Boksanica?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as navigation is concerned, but the distance was very small and we knew this recently very well, even without looking at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue. It's not much, I hope, if we've done it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We've fast forwarded it now. Do you recognise where you're approaching to now?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise this. On the previous part of the footage, which you fast forwarded so it didn't explain it, we approached the region of Boksanica but we were at the foot of the mountain. This is where we landed, and the general explained that there was quite a large distance to walk up the hill and that the helicopter would be insecure if left there, if we were going to accompany him, so one of us would have to stay by the helicopter. And this is why he told the pilot to takeoff again and to try and land higher up on Boksanica. He supposed that there would be enough room there, and here on the footage, you could see the pilot indicating with his hand. And this is why we moved and landed in this field near Boksanica. And in the back there you can see the white roof of the check-point, UN-manned check-point, so where we landed this is the space of some 100 to 150 metres, and on the right-hand side of the helicopter, on this picture that you can see right now, there was a road; on the left-hand side there was a wood path by these pine trees, and there is also a monument to an UN soldier that was killed there because he stepped on a mine. I believe it was a Ukrainian UN soldier. So I believe this is the first time that we arrived to Boksanica during the times of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that was going to be my question. Given that you're getting your bearings and figuring out the best place to land, that would indicate this was your first helicopter visit there; correct?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct, this was the first time we came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's let it go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you -- were you around General Mladic when he went into the comms tent there and was trying to get ahold of Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present. He wasn't -- he wasn't in a tent, but, rather, in a log house and in a container that was there, so one part of that particular facility was a log cabin and one was this container, and he entered there because the radio station was there through which he got into communication with, I assume, the Muslim forces in Zepa or, possibly, with Ukrainian unit. Later on, he did not enter but he stayed outside. The tables for negotiations were outside. And I was by his side all the time together with Major Maran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. Let's just continue with some brief segments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you -- if you remember, can you explain what just happened? If you don't remember, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to pick up General Tolimir. I assume the negotiations were about to start, so the General wanted to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you and the pilot went back and got General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I came back as well, possibly. I cannot recall that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you know Colonel -- Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, do you remember him, the fellow with a big mustache?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him, and he was around in those days. This is the first time I saw him. I didn't know who he was. Previously, I saw him in these days, and later on, after the operation, I didn't see him anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is the fellah behind General Mladic, if you can tell?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Major Dusan Maran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is there on the left side of the screen next to Major Maran and behind General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the persons that were escorting General Mladic. I believe his name was Zrnic, and I believe he was from Sarajevo, that is all I know. I didn't know him too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The person on the far left of the screen, the person with the dark hair, isn't that you?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's me, while I had dark hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's at 00.02.24. So let's keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, and here we are again, 00.03.02 and that's you again on the left side of the screen stepping right in front of the camera lens.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the rare moments. I could not flee from the general. I initially told you that there was a minefield around this place, which we do not know specifically where it was, so I could not roam the wider area. I kept close to them, and, of course, it was inevitable for me to appear on the screen, especially so because the general may issue, at any moment, a task to me. And another reason is that only the three of us were there as security detail for the general. It was possible for somebody to open fire from the woods. We were the first time there on that location. We didn't even know where the Muslim positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can just finish it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We are going to be done pretty quick, sir. There is one other area I wanted to ask you about, and that is something -- a statement you said, this was at page 33919, and you said: "General Gvero came there because he wanted to discuss some issues with General Mladic because for several days he'd been unable to get in touch with him because the General was avoiding contact with any officers that were not working on Zepa; or, more specifically, the Boksanica thing." So I want to explore with you this issue of whether or not General Gvero was actually working on Zepa prior to this time. And the first thing I would like to do is go to the exhibit 65 ter 2747. That's an UN report. But I'll perhaps remind you of a -- do you remember a meeting between General Mladic and General Gvero and General Smith at the Jela restaurant on 25 July, the day before you were in Boksanica? And let's go to -- well, excuse me now. Let's just look at paragraph 1 of this report, which is dated 26 July. And it says: "General Smith met General Mladic at 'restaurant Jela' at Hans-Kram at 1230 hours on 25 July 1995. The meeting was at our request. Our purpose was to discuss the situation in Zepa and also to follow-up on aspects of the agreement signed between General Smith and General Mladic on 19 July. General Mladic was accompanied by General Gvero." And also this document goes on and says that General Mladic arrived in a helicopter. So that must have been you that took General Mladic to that meeting. So surely you remember General Mladic, General Gvero, and General Smith meeting about -- at the Jela restaurant, the day before the material you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that if he arrived there by helicopter to the area of the Jela restaurant, then it must have been us who transported them. I don't know what they discussed. I cannot tell you with certainty that General Gvero was there as well. I knew that General Smith was there because I spoke to his associate standing outside. We could not see what was going on in there. They may as well have been drinking coffee and tell us later that they had negotiations, but I don't recall what they discussed. I wasn't privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to another exhibit, P00191.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is that same day, and just to -- July 25. It's a document sent, as a you'll see, to the Main Staff of the VRS on the 25th of July to General Gvero or General Miletic, and it's from General Tolimir, and it's entitled: "Agreement on Disarmament of Zepa." I won't go into it details of it since you don't know the details, but clearly you can see from this document it's related to the same subject matter of the Jela restaurant meeting, and it would show that General Gvero was an interested party in Zepa; wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document. First, I will have to read it to be able to interpret it. I cannot confirm something that I've never seen in my life. If it was addressed to him or to General Miletic, well, maybe the reason for that was that they were the only ones at the moment in the operations room of the Main Staff, all the other generals being out in the field. It can be seen from the first sentence, We send you this to forward to another corps command to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, so they are giving them a courier's task. As for the rest of the document, I can't comment on it because I've never read it and it would be serious for me to try to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's look at P01333. And this is the English version, but we shouldn't -- we shouldn't broadcast it. This is an intercepted conversation that was intercepted on 25 July; A is the English, C is the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the time of this conversation was 0945 hours. And the previous document had a receipt of 0530 hours. So a few hours later we have a conversation where, at the end of the conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 133 A -- sorry, 1333 A; A and C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see from the end of the intercept that the intercept operators concluded that X was, in fact, Milan Gvero. And so if we look at this intercept, mid-way down the first page in both languages, we can see that General Gvero, when asked in what condition are they up there? He says: "Good, very good. They signed the agreement last night related to the surrender of Zepa." Then there is some talk, and they go on, and if we look at page 2. And in the English it's -- there is a little talk about Glamoc, but we can tell from this that General Gvero is certainly informed of the agreement, the important agreement, that's gone on in Zepa. So let me show you another intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's P1334.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Saying let's not send this out. A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is between General Milan Gvero and a fellah named Subara. It's on 25 July, a little later now at 0950 hours. And again, I just want to call your attention to what Subara is concerned about, what's going on in the media on Zepa and Srebrenica. And again, General Gvero talks about, as we can see from the first few lines, that an agreement was signed last night. We are going to allow everything. If they are smart, the ICRC will control it and an UNPROFOR representative will also be present. It talks about some more of the details, I won't go in it, but if this is an accurate intercept, you will agree with me that this shows that General Gvero, despite what you have said, was certainly knowledgeable in the events that were going on in Zepa at the time?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is the first time I see those two documents. You read through them so quickly I could not read them. I cannot agree with you about something that I see for the first time and have not studied. Person X could be many other people, not just General Gvero. I could have been that person, X. We all spoke on the phone. I don't know which intercepted conversation this was about. I started to read the letterhead and you started asking questions about me agreeing with something that I have not had an opportunity to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Krgovic, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That brings your testimony to an end here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence at such short notice, and I also wish you, on behalf of everyone, a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer 1333 A, the intercept, and then the video-clip 4590.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? We hear none. They are -- wasn't the first one already admitted or ... Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm told it was not. It may have been, I thought it was, but I'm told it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It's just a vague impression that I had. All right. They are so admitted. That brings to an end your list of witnesses, I take it, Mr. Krgovic, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, just so I don't lose track, it's A, B, and C so that we get all languages in that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay that's how I understood you anyway. Thank you. You don't have any further witnesses? I'm addressing the Gvero Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, no we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we stand adjourned. There is a sitting fixed for Thursday, this Thursday, for the hearing of the Nikolic witness, if he turns up. Otherwise, we will have other proceedings to be notified later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of July, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.17 a.m.,
